paragraphs: One must weigh with a generous eye (favorably to the buyer), as it is said (Deuteronomy 25:15), "A perfect and just weight shall you have" — give him a bit extra from your own (Bava Batra 88b). Likewise one must measure with a generous eye, as it is said, "a perfect and just measure," etc. And how much is a 'generous eye'? One part in a hundred for liquids and one part in four hundred for dry goods, since liquid clings [to the vessel]. All this measure applies where the custom is to weigh exactly; but where the custom is to 'tip the scale,' one is obligated to tip it a handbreadth for foods and drinks, though for other items a small tip suffices, provided it is one part in four hundred. And if the quantity is less than a litra, even for foods and drinks one need not tip a handbreadth. Now here in our city of Baghdad there is no clear custom in this matter; therefore one should be careful to give at least this measure — one part in a hundred for liquids and one part in four hundred for dry goods.

clarification.explanation: One must weigh and measure with a 'generous eye' — giving a little extra — as it is said, "a perfect and just weight ... a perfect and just measure." The measure of the generous eye: one part in a hundred for liquids and one part in four hundred for dry goods (since liquid clings [to the vessel]). This applies where the custom is to weigh precisely; where the custom is to 'tip the scale' (tilt the pan), one is obligated to tip it a handbreadth for foods and drinks, and for other items a small tip suffices, provided it equals one part in four hundred; and for less than a litra, no handbreadth tip is required. In Baghdad there is no clear custom, so one should be careful to give at least one part in a hundred for liquids and one part in four hundred for dry goods.
takeaways: One measures and weighs with a generous eye — giving a small extra amount.
At least one part in a hundred for liquids and one part in four hundred for dry goods.

paragraphs: Anyone who keeps in his house or shop a deficient weight or a deficient measure transgresses a prohibition (Deuteronomy 25:13), as it is said, "You shall not have in your bag a large stone and a small one" — and even if he never actually measures with it, he still transgresses. Thus this prohibition applies to him even at the time of the Ne'ilah prayer on Yom Kippur. The same law applies to a similar case: one should not keep a paid promissory note [that has not been destroyed], nor keep a copper coin plated with silver and the like.

clarification.explanation: Anyone who keeps in his house or shop a deficient weight or a deficient measure transgresses a prohibition ("You shall not have in your bag a large stone and a small one"), and even if he never measures with them at all — mere possession is a transgression — so that he transgresses this prohibition even during the Ne'ilah prayer on Yom Kippur. Likewise, one should not keep a promissory note that has already been paid, nor a copper coin plated with silver and the like (deceptive items).
takeaways: It is forbidden even merely to possess deficient weights/measures (or a paid note and a counterfeit coin) — a continuous transgression.

paragraphs: The Torah was strict about weights and measures in any amount whatsoever: one who weighs with a weight or measure deficient from the local custom, even a small amount, transgresses the prohibition, "You shall not do unrighteousness in judgment, in measure, in weight, or in volume" (Leviticus 19:35). And our Sages of blessed memory said (Yevamot 21a) that the punishment for [dishonesty in] weights and measures is more severe than that for forbidden relations, because this robs the public and he does not know to whom to make restitution; and even though it is said that he should use [the ill-gotten gain] for public needs, this is not a proper remedy.

clarification.explanation: The Torah was strict about weights and measures in any amount: one who weighs or measures deficiently from the local custom, even a small amount, transgresses a prohibition ("You shall not do unrighteousness in judgment, in measure, in weight, or in volume"). And the Sages said that the punishment for [dishonesty in] weights and measures is more severe than for forbidden relations, because he robs the public and does not know to whom to make restitution; and even if he uses the money for public needs, this is not a proper remedy.
takeaways: Any deficiency in measure is a transgression of a prohibition.
More severe than forbidden relations, because it robs the public with no way to make restitution.

paragraphs: Although it was said that weights should not be made of metal but only of smooth stone, nevertheless nowadays it is customary to make metal weights according to government regulation, since the government makes them with its own seal and issues them to whoever needs them; thus everyone relies upon and accepts them as such. Therefore, even though over time they wear down slightly, everyone knows this and accepts it. However, shopkeepers who sell sesame oil in a measuring vessel that they own — this vessel, over the course of time, accumulates dregs like thick mud on its bottom and sides, which necessarily makes the measurement deficient; therefore the shopkeeper must clean it thoroughly twice a week from all the dregs that stick and collect in it, since he sells constantly. But those who have a place called in Arabic 'bazara' (an oil press, for producing oil) — where they process the oil and sell it to shopkeepers in a large vessel called in Arabic 'farg' (a large glass container for liquids) — these do not sell and measure with this vessel constantly like the shopkeeper does, and moreover their custom is to leave the [measuring] vessel inverted over the buyer's container after the flow has stopped, until three drops drip from it. Therefore it is possible that these have the law of a wholesaler, about whom our Rabbis of blessed memory said (Bava Batra 87a) that he must wipe out liquid measures once every thirty days.

clarification.explanation: Although it was said that weights should not be made of metal, nowadays it is customary to make metal weights bearing the government's seal, and since everyone knows and accepts this — it is permitted, even though over time they wear down slightly. But a shopkeeper who sells sesame oil in a measuring vessel in which dregs accumulate at the bottom and sides (causing the measurement to be deficient) must clean it thoroughly twice a week, since he sells constantly. Owners of an oil press who sell wholesale in a large vessel and do not measure with it constantly (and also leave the vessel inverted until three drops drip out) — their law is like that of a wholesaler, who cleans liquid measures once every thirty days.
takeaways: Metal weights bearing the government's seal are permitted even though they wear down slightly.
One must clean a measuring vessel of dregs (a shopkeeper twice a week; a wholesaler about once a month) so the measurement not be deficient.

paragraphs: A shopkeeper who weighs something moist, such as fresh dates or meat and the like, must wipe the scale-pan into which he places the moist item each time he weighs with it; he must also wipe the weight itself once a week, because the shopkeeper's hands become soiled with moisture, and this soils the weight and makes it heavier due to the accumulated grime. And although if it becomes heavier this is a loss to the shopkeeper and a benefit to the buyer, they required this of him because sometimes the shopkeeper himself buys something and weighs it with that same weight, and thus he would be robbing [the seller]. Maimonides of blessed memory (Hilchot Geneivah, ch. 8, halachah 18), however, gave the reason that it is so that rust should not form from the grime, for if rust forms, the weight becomes deficient.

clarification.explanation: A shopkeeper who weighs something moist (fresh dates, meat, and the like) must wipe the scale-pan every time he weighs, and must also wipe the weight itself once a week — because his hands, soiled with moisture, soil the weight and make it heavier. Although making the weight heavier is a loss to the shopkeeper and a gain to the buyer, they required this because sometimes the shopkeeper himself buys and weighs with it, and would thereby be robbing [the seller]; and Maimonides gave the reason that it prevents rust from forming from the grime (which would also make it deficient).
takeaways: One wipes the scale-pan each time a moist item is weighed, and the weight itself once a week, in order to preserve accuracy.

paragraphs: Even one who weighs or measures with any deficiency at all for a non-Jew transgresses a prohibition and must make restitution, because he is deceiving him, and this is actual theft; and this falls under "for whoever does these things, whoever does unrighteousness, is an abomination to the Lord your God" — which comes to include one who does unrighteousness to a non-Jew (Bava Batra 88a). And it is found in Tanna d'vei Eliyahu of blessed memory (ch. 15), cited in the Yalkut on parashat Tzav, that Eliyahu of blessed memory said: A certain man came and sat before me; he knew Scripture but not Mishnah. He said to me: Rabbi, it once happened that I sold a non-Jew four kor of dates and measured them out to him in a dark house, half [light] and half [dark]. He said to me, 'You and the God in Heaven know with what measure you are measuring for me' — and I shorted him three se'ah of dates in the measuring. Afterward I took the money and bought with it a jug of oil, and I placed it in the spot where I had sold the dates, and the jug cracked and spilled out. I said to him: Blessed is the Omnipresent, blessed is He who shows no favoritism — Scripture says (Leviticus 19:13), "You shall not oppress your fellow, nor rob him," and robbing a non-Jew is forbidden, and they explained elsewhere (Ezekiel 18:18) "for he practiced oppression, oppression" [doubling to include a non-Jew]. Thus far his words.

clarification.explanation: Even one who weighs or measures with any deficiency at all for a non-Jew transgresses a prohibition and must make restitution, because he deceives him and this is actual theft, and it falls under "whoever does unrighteousness," which includes unrighteousness done to a non-Jew. (Rabbi Yosef Chaim brings a story from Eliyahu the Prophet about a man who shorted a non-Jew in a measurement and lost his profit as a result.)
takeaways: Dishonesty in measure or weight is forbidden and requires restitution even toward a non-Jew — it is actual theft.

paragraphs: It is forbidden by Torah law to steal or rob anything at all, whether from a Jew or from a non-Jew, whether from a great person or a small one, and even if the non-Jew caused distress to a Jew. Robbing a non-Jew is especially serious: first, because he certainly will not forgive it; and further, because it causes the [heavenly] prince of that nation to steal and rob, measure for measure, from the holy flow of abundance that flows down to Israel from above — and there are deep matters involved in this. Therefore one must be very careful.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden by Torah law to steal or rob anything at all — whether from a Jew or a non-Jew, whether from a great person or a small one, even if the non-Jew caused distress to a Jew. Robbing a non-Jew is especially severe: he certainly will not forgive it, and it also causes the [heavenly] prince of that nation to 'rob' from above the holy flow of abundance that comes to Israel, measure for measure. Therefore one must be very careful.
takeaways: Robbery of any amount is forbidden by Torah law from anyone.
Robbing a non-Jew is especially severe (he will not forgive, and it causes spiritual harm).

paragraphs: Although less than the value of a perutah is not considered 'money' and need not be restored, nevertheless we hold that 'half the measure' is forbidden by Torah law (Yoma 73b, Chullin 98a). And if it is something so minor that people ordinarily do not mind about it, such as taking a splinter from a bundle of wood or from a fence to pick one's teeth with, this is permitted; nevertheless it is a measure of piety to refrain and be careful even about this. But one who enters his fellow's house and takes with his hand a splinter from a hand-fan made of woven wind, called in Arabic 'marwacha' (a fan woven from palm-branch leaves), which is a vessel woven from lulav leaves used for fanning oneself in the summer heat — even though the splinter is a very minor thing, nevertheless it damages and diminishes that marwacha from which the splinter is taken, and the owners certainly do mind about this, and it is forbidden by law — except if it was already old and broken, in which case there is no loss to it if one takes a piece of splinter from it to pick one's teeth. In any case, it is a measure of piety to be careful about this too, and one must warn the people about this matter also in the synagogue during the summer months, where such vessels called marwacha are kept ready, being consecrated property [hekdesh], so that there is a loss to hekdesh in this — and who will forgive it?

clarification.explanation: Although less than the value of a perutah is not 'money' that must be restored, 'half the measure' is forbidden by Torah law. Something so minor that people ordinarily do not mind about (taking a splinter from a bundle of wood or a fence to pick one's teeth with) is permitted, and it is a measure of piety to be careful even about this. But one who takes a splinter from a fan woven of lulav leaves (marwacha) — even though the splinter is minor, it damages and diminishes the fan, and its owners do mind, so it is forbidden by law (unless it is already old and broken). And in the synagogue, such fans are consecrated property [hekdesh] — and who will forgive that loss? Therefore the people must be warned about this.
takeaways: Taking something so minor that no one minds is permitted (though a pious person is careful even about this).
But if the taking damages an item (like a fan), or the item is consecrated property, it is forbidden.

paragraphs: Here in our city, Arab women bring vessels full of thickened soured milk, called in Arabic 'laban' and in another language 'yogurt,' in order to sell it, and their custom is to taste it first with their finger to know if it is good, and then to buy. But there are people who do not wish to buy at all, yet pretend that they wish to buy, in order to taste from every single vessel; and after each and every tasting they say that it did not please them, and they leave without buying anything. This is forbidden, for it constitutes deceiving people [geneivat da'at], and it is also theft in his hand. For even though he tastes only a small amount from each vessel, nevertheless the owner of the laban forgives the tasting only to one who genuinely wishes to buy.

clarification.explanation: In Baghdad, Arab women sell thickened soured milk (laban/yogurt), and their custom is to let people taste it first to check it. Some people pretend they wish to buy only in order to taste from every vessel, and after each tasting say it did not please them and leave without buying — this is a transgression of deceiving people [geneivat da'at] and also theft in their hand, since the seller forgives the tasting only to one who genuinely intends to buy.
takeaways: Tasting merchandise under the pretense of buying, without any real intention to buy, is deceiving people and theft.

paragraphs: One whose shoes were exchanged in the synagogue or elsewhere: if the one who made the exchange did so deliberately — for instance, taking a new shoe and leaving an old one — then it is permitted to use the shoe he left behind. But if the first one made the exchange inadvertently, without noticing — for instance, the shoes were of equal value, or he took the inferior one and left the better one, in which case it clearly appears he acted inadvertently — then it is forbidden to use it; rather, it must remain with him until its owner comes and it is given to him.

clarification.explanation: One whose shoes were exchanged in the synagogue or elsewhere: if the one who exchanged them did so deliberately (took a new shoe and left an old one) — it is permitted to use the shoe he left behind. But if the exchange happened inadvertently (the shoes were equal in value, or he took the inferior one and left the better one) — it is forbidden to use it; rather, it must be kept until its owner comes and it is given to him.
takeaways: If shoes were exchanged deliberately (to your disadvantage) — you may use the one left behind.
If inadvertently — it is forbidden; keep it until the owner comes.

paragraphs: It is forbidden to mix a small amount of inferior produce into a large quantity of good produce in a way that it is not recognizable, in order to sell the whole as good produce. However, any produce or grain that has waste matter or dust mixed into it, even pebbles and stones, if they became mixed in by themselves, one need not sort them out; it is only mixing them in deliberately by hand that is forbidden.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to mix a small amount of inferior produce into a large quantity of good produce in a way that is not noticeable, in order to sell the whole as good. But produce or grain that has waste, dust, or even pebbles and stones mixed in on their own need not be sorted out; only deliberately mixing them in by hand is forbidden.
takeaways: It is forbidden to deliberately conceal inferior merchandise within good merchandise.
Waste that got mixed in on its own is not a problem, but deliberate mixing is forbidden.

paragraphs: It is forbidden to deceive people [geneivat da'at] even in matters that involve no loss, merely in order that they should feel grateful to him for nothing. How so? He should not press his fellow to dine with him when he knows that he will not dine [with him]. But without pressing, it is permitted to say it once or twice even though he knows that the other has no intention of eating with him, for this is an honor paid to him — showing him respect through an invitation, in accordance with proper etiquette.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to deceive people even in matters involving no loss, when one does so merely so that they should feel grateful to him for nothing. How so? He should not press his fellow to dine with him when he knows the other will not dine with him; but without pressing, it is permitted to invite him once or twice even knowing he will not eat with him, since this is an honor paid to him in accordance with proper etiquette.
takeaways: It is forbidden to create false gratitude (insincere pressing/insistence).
A polite invitation once or twice, without pressing, is permitted.

paragraphs: Just as there is wrongful deception [ona'ah] in commerce, so too there is wrongful deception in words, and wrongful deception in words is greater than wrongful deception in money — for the latter can be restored and the former cannot be restored; the one affects his body and the other his money. And all the more so if one curses, demeans, or shames him. And one who calls his fellow by a derogatory nickname — even if that person is accustomed to that nickname and is not embarrassed by it — if the intent is to shame him, it is forbidden on account of wrongful deception in words.

clarification.explanation: Just as there is wrongful deception [ona'ah] in commerce, so there is wrongful deception in words, and wrongful deception in words is worse than wrongful deception in money: the latter can be restored and the former cannot; one harms the body, the other the money — and all the more so one who curses, demeans, and shames. And one who calls his fellow by a derogatory nickname — even if the person is accustomed to it and is not embarrassed — if the intent is to shame him, it is forbidden as wrongful deception in words.
takeaways: Hurting someone with words is worse than hurting them financially (it cannot be undone).
A derogatory nickname meant to shame is forbidden, even if the victim is used to it.

paragraphs: It is forbidden to throw a carcass in the public domain, in the lanes within the city — such as a dead chicken or cat, or a rotting fish, and the like. And it is a mitzvah upon anyone who sees a reeking carcass in the streets of the city to pay someone a wage for his trouble to carry it outside the city, and this is considered a matter of public need. This is especially so according to the view of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory (Sha'ar Ruach HaKodesh, 8), who warned very strongly that a person should not smell the stench of a carcass, for this is very harmful even to the soul. And there are people who, in order to spare the cesspit in their courtyards, called in Arabic 'bal'uah' (a drainage pit), do not pour water into it, and so pour out into the public domain all the foul water that occurs in their house, and its stench reaches passersby who are disgusted by it — and these people are destined to give a reckoning for this. And it is also known what is written in the holy Zohar concerning those who pour foul and disgusting water in front of the entrance of their courtyard — that they are cursed by the mouths of the angels. This is the general rule: anything that a person is disgusted by and finds repulsive within his own house, he should not pour or throw it into the public domain.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to throw a carcass (a dead chicken or cat, a rotting fish, and the like) into the streets and lanes of the city, and it is a mitzvah for one who sees a reeking carcass in the city streets to pay someone to remove it outside the city (this is a matter of public need), especially according to the Ari, who warned strongly that a person should not smell the stench of a carcass (which is harmful even to the soul). And there are those who, to spare their courtyard's drainage pit, pour foul water into the public domain instead, and its stench reaches passersby — and they are destined to give a reckoning for this. The holy Zohar also states that those who pour foul and disgusting water in front of their courtyard's entrance are cursed by the mouths of the angels. The general rule: anything a person is disgusted by and finds repulsive in his own house, he should not pour or throw into the public domain.
takeaways: It is forbidden to throw a carcass or foul water into the public domain; it is a mitzvah to remove a stench from the street.
Whatever disgusts you in your own home — do not pour it into the public domain.
The holy Zohar warns that those who pour foul water in front of their courtyard's entrance are cursed by the mouths of the angels.

paragraphs: One who builds his house, even though he is permitted to place the dirt and stones in the public domain according to local custom, nevertheless should not leave dirt and stones that he has no need of for the building and that he will eventually clear away — should not leave them for a long time so that passersby stumble over them, but should clear them away immediately. And a person should not say: Who is stopping me, who will complain against me, who sees me, if I throw a carcass or something foul into the public domain at night in the dark? Rather, in truth, a person must be his own judge, and place the fear of Heaven before him, and know that for everything God will bring a person to judgment. Our Rabbis of blessed memory said (Bava Kamma 50b): There was an incident involving a man who was removing stones from his courtyard and throwing them into the public domain. A certain pious man came upon him and said to him: Why are you clearing stones from a domain that is not yours into a domain that is yours? That homeowner mocked him, [thinking to himself that] he considers the courtyard his and the public domain not his. Afterward, not many days passed before that man was forced to sell his courtyard; he sold it, and [later,] walking through that same lane, he stumbled over those very stones that he himself had cleared away, and fell to the ground. He said: That pious man spoke well. Therefore one must be very careful about these matters, and it is good for him [to be so].

clarification.explanation: One who builds his house is indeed permitted, according to local custom, to place dirt and stones in the public domain, but dirt and stones that he does not need for the building and will eventually remove — he should not leave for a long time so that passersby stumble over them, but should clear them away at once. And a person should not say, 'Who sees me if I throw a carcass or something foul into the public domain at night in the dark' — rather, he must be his own judge, place the fear of Heaven before him, and know that God brings everyone to judgment for everything. (A story is brought of a man who threw stones from his courtyard into the public domain, and after he sold his courtyard he himself stumbled over those very stones.)
takeaways: Unneeded building debris must be cleared from the public domain immediately.
One should not rely on 'who is watching' — God judges everything; what harms the public comes back upon the person himself.
